subject: humanities
passage: Through most of the seventeenth century, church organs in northern Europe were commonly tuned in meantone temperament, a system that makes the most frequently used keys sound especially sweet but makes keys with many sharps or flats sound harshly out of tune. Retuning an organ was slow and costly work, so an organist usually had to accept whatever tuning his instrument already had. Musicologist Anke Brandt notes that organ music by northern German composers of the 1600s rarely uses those remote keys. She argues that this pattern reflects the limits of the instruments the composers played rather than a shared taste for simpler keys.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's argument?

choices.A: Organists whose instruments were retuned to newer systems soon began writing organ works in remote keys.
choices.B: Meantone tuning was also common on church organs in Italy and England during the 1600s.
choices.C: Most northern German organ music of the 1600s is written in keys that have few sharps or flats.
choices.D: The same composers' unaccompanied choral works, which were free of any fixed tuning, also avoided remote keys.

explanation.why: Brandt says the composers avoided remote keys because their organs could not play them well, not because they disliked such keys. The best support would show the composers' choices changing when only the instrument's tuning changed. Organists who began using remote keys once their organs were retuned show that the tuning, not their taste, had held them back.
explanation.A: Correct. When the tuning limit was removed, the same organists began writing in remote keys, showing that the instruments, not taste, had restricted them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Where else meantone tuning was used says nothing about why these composers avoided remote keys.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This simply restates the pattern Brandt is trying to explain; it does not show whether the instruments or the composers' taste caused it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Avoiding remote keys even where no tuning limited them would suggest a shared taste for simpler keys; this weakens the argument.
